messages.subject: Using pre-post factor scores in mixed regression
messages.subject_clean: Using pre-post factor scores in mixed regression
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am conducting an analysis where I analyze potential sex differences in pre and post classroom anxiety and how these differences predict pre and post semester IQ scores. For this analysis, I am using the Mirt package in R.

Initially, I had polytomous  data with five categories( were the first category is a non-endorsement and the other four were increasing degrees of endorsement, ex. “A little”, “A fair amount”, “Much”, and “Very Much”); however, I encountered numerous estimation issues for item parameters due to low endorsement of the third to fifth categories. Consequently, I read the literature and decided to convert my polytomous data into binary data by collapsing the four endorsement categories into a single endorsement category and simply comparing non-endorsers to endorsers. I recognize that I lose information; however, my analysis went much smoother. Additionally, I have used the DETECT function in sort and my pre data meets the unidimensional requirement for an irt analysis.

Ultimately, to derive the factor scores while accounting for random effects and the correlation among pre and post data, I have used the mixedmirt function (with the default Rasch itemtype ) and used sex as a fixed effect to account for uniform DIF and used participants ID to estimate each individual’s random effects. I finally then used the randef function to obtain my theta scores with uniform sex DIF accounted for. These scores were then used to analyze the interaction of sex and factor anxiety scores on pre and post IQ scores in lmer.

With that background, my issue is accounting for the uniform DIF caused by time. Initially, I used the multiple group function to analyze which item intercepts were statistically different in the pre and post group and eliminate them prior to the multilevel irt; however, I have read that in multilevel/longitudinal irt, the intercept is the fixed time effect. So, ultimately, for those who are more experienced with IRT, can you please offer insight on my current analysis? Are there any studies that you can point me to ultimately better my analysis?

Thank you for the assistance!

messages.subject: Reverse coding of some items within a scale: only flip a? or both a and d-parameters? Or take 1-P?
messages.subject_clean: Reverse coding of some items within a scale: only flip a? or both a and d-parameters? Or take 1-P?
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I have done a calibration of a set of 2PL items (originally they were Likert items but for a special application I dichotimized the variables), I reverse coded the negatively worded items before the calibration.

Now for calculated expected item responses (probabilities) I would like to have the signed itemparameters (i.e., indicating that a higher score decreases the probability of endorsing an item).

Reading on this forum I read that people solve this by simply multiplying the a-parameter by -1. This flips the item characteristic function, but not as I would have expected. My guess would have been to just use the expected item probabilities and subtract it from one (i.e., 1-P). And I found out that this can by achieved by flipping both the a and d-parameter.

So now I am confused as to what to do, i.e. what is the correct way of going about this, multiplying only the a-parameter by -1 or simply taking the old calibration as a starting point and take 1-P for the reverse items.

I have provided some R code below that different approaches yield different (or similar) results. The code below essentially calculates expected item probabilities (it is a multidimensional 2PL model with 2 traits), I calculate an expected prob for a medium score (theta = 0) and high (theta=4) score.

# these are the parameters I got after my calibration (before which I reverse coded items)
a=1.842
d=0.342

theta_mid<-c(0,0)
theta_hi<-c(4,0)

1/ (1+exp(-1*(c(a,0)%*%theta_mid+ d))) # 0.5846763
1/ (1+exp(-1*(c(a,0)%*%theta_hi+ d))) #  0.9995519

# only flipping a
1/ (1+exp(-1*(c(-a,0)%*%theta_mid+ d))) #0.5846763  NOTE THAT THIS IS THE SAME EXPECTED PROB AS ABOVE
1/ (1+exp(-1*(c(-a,0)%*%theta_hi+ d))) #0.0008876899 this is different

# only flipping d
1/ (1+exp(-1*(c(a,0)%*%theta_mid+ -d))) #0.4153237 (NOTE THAT THIS IS 1 MINUS the above 0.5846763 prob)
1/ (1+exp(-1*(c(a,0)%*%theta_hi+ -d))) #0.9991123 (NOTE THAT THIS IS 1 MINUS the above .000887 prob)

# flipping both a and d
1/ (1+exp(-1*(c(-a,0)%*%theta_mid+ -d))) # 0.4153237 (SAME AS ONLY FLIPPING D AND 1-0.5846763 )
1/ (1+exp(-1*(c(-a,0)%*%theta_hi+ -d))) # 0.0004481206 (SAME AS 1-0.9995519 FROM ABOVE)

messages.subject_clean: First Year Graduate Student Seeking Advice
messages.body_plain:
Hi Donisha,

On Mon, Jul 20, 2020 at 9:00 PM Donisha Smith <dsmi...@fiu.edu> wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> As the title states, I am a first year graduate student and am currently attempting to conduct data analysis for my Master's project. I haven't taken many courses so I had to resort to studying item response theory on my own. My goal is to obtain valid scores from an anxiety assessment, which was administered at pre-treatment and post-treatment,so is a repeated measure, to use in linear mixed model and assess gender differences in anxiety at baseline and analyze potential gender differences in anxiety changes over time. So, because I am a novice, I wanted to draw on someone's expertise with the mirt package to ensure thatI am using the package correctly:
>
> 1) From my understanding of irt with polytomous, item difficulties are the average of the observed responses divided by the maximum possible response.

That's perhaps a definition based on observations only, and sounds more akin to what one would find in classical test theory item analyses. In IRT difficulty/intercept parameters are estimated from a model given the available response data, so you won't get this type of definition.

> Let's say I have 20 items in my assessment, all which have a maximum of 4 categories with 0 being the lowest, but at baseline, participants are less likely to endorse higher categories, how exactly do I use the customK function to let the package the true total number of categories in each question?

You could supply the value of 5 to the customK function for these items, but I would highly advise against this. Categories not observed are not identifiable, so if you tried to estimate the parameters associated with missing categories you'll obtain meaningless parameters, and the model will fail to converge.

>
> 2) I'm aware that if I want to compare participants across time, I have to ensure measurement invariance, where items are functioning similarly among participants with the similar latent abilities; however, because my ultimate goal is to compare gender differences across time. My idea is to conduct differential item functioning between males and females at baseline, eliminate items that show a gender bias, then conduct differential item functioning between  the baseline group (combined male and female) with themselves at post treatment to eliminate longitudinal item bias. I have looked at the literature extensively but most studies either perform DIF between groups only or perform DIF across time only. So, I wanted to know if my idea is reasonable.

The idea seems reasonable enough to me if this is indeed your research purpose.

>
> 3) From my understanding, anchoring items for DIF can result in misleading fit statistics; however, is the opposite true? Where undercutting items can lead to a poor DIF analysis? Since the DIF and the multipleGroup function identifies 'n' number of groups and scales the groups to be equated for DIF. I believe that I should first conduct separate/individual single class models for baseline males and females and analyze item fits separately for both group and select the overlapping "good" fitting items to use in baseline DIF for males and females and to use in the longitudinal DIF.

That's also reasonable. You wouldn't want to compare groups across anchored models if within the groups the models fit poorly.

>
> 4) (I promise this is the last question). I also have a bit of missing data in my pre condition and my post condition (approximately 4% in each). My idea was to conduct conduct the baseline and longitudinal DIF first and once I can assure that all items have good fit and display no bias, then I can use the imputeMissing function on the longitudinal multipleGroup model with anchored intercepts and slopes to  generate the missing scores.

Missing data shouldn't pose much of an issue in mirt since the estimation algorithms are all full-information based. Unless you have outside information about how to plausibly generate the response absent the fitted IRT models then it's best to just leave the missing data as-is and rely on assumptions such as 'missing at random'.

>
> Admittedly, I have been experimenting with the package extensively and have been adjusting the latent distribution since their is evidence that the distribution is non normal and conducting DIF(which.par = c('a1', 'd'), scheme = 'drop') to analyze the slope and intercepts jointly. But I'm not entirely confident in my analysis plan. Some of you are probably wondering why I don't ask my mentor but I am in a neuroscience program so many do not emphasize the behavioral statistics. Additionally, due to the epidemic, professors in different departments haven't been responding to my requests. I just want to construct a reliable behavioral model so that I can transition into creating a neural model knowing that my behavioral model is valid.

Trying times for all. Good luck.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Integration of ShinyApp with MirtCat
messages.body_plain:
The mirtCAT() interface generally assumes you know the important demographic information a priori so that you can organize the CAT session specifically for the population of interest. I have not developed the 'demographic' pages too much for this very reason. What you could do is run a Shiny-type survey to obtain your data, save the data somewhere accessible (on a hard-drive or server), and at the end of your survey provide a link to a mirtCAT session that is capable of reading in this information. Then, using the inputs like the customNextItem() function you could select items based on the saved criteria (other variants of this idea are possible as well, such as generating a unique link at the end of your initial survey that already points to the correct CAT interface). HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
You shouldn't need to include an ID variable to do this since the mixedmirt() setup already assumes that the individuals are random effect terms (and are treated specially as they are actually complex in that they could be mixed with fixed slope coefficients). This type of setup makes mixedmirt() more/less flexible in some cases.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
mirt doesn't currently support this pairwise estimation algorithm; it is restricted to marginal ML/Baysian estimation only. Regarding your questions, from what I can tell the algorithm is just using different count tables to compute the parameters, which has it's advantages/disadvantages like all other approaches (could be impeller to implement than CML estimation, for instance, and may avoid the use of a prior ability distribution which is required for MML estimation). Is there some reason you prefer using this algorithm verses CML (available in the eRm package) and MML (available in mirt)?

Phil

Hi Dr. Phil,

I wanted to thank you for answering my questions (especially the one seeking advice). Your package has also made the analysis process exciting and lead to learn more flexible techniques in item analysis. I've read articles regarding the RPRI model and most dichotomize their scales to apply a Rasch RPRI model. With the polytomous data, I have to consider threshold shifts and discrimination shifts as opposed to a single intercept shift in a 1PL model. I have looked at older articles
from David Andrich and others debating the validity of the joining adjacent categories and possible violations of invariance. I have conducted my analysis with the original polytomous data. I have also dichotomized my data by categorizing "Not at all" as "0" a non-endorsement and categorized "A little", "A fair amount", "Much", and "Very Much" as endorsements or "1". I lose the gradations among the endorsers; however, I can model longitudinal uniform DIF and random intercepts while constraining the discrimination parameter and derive the pre and post factor scores. From my perspective, in the pre and post conditions, the 4th and 5th categories were rarely endorsed and mirt rescores my data due to skipped categories. Additionally, the graded response model is essentially cumulative/sequential 2pl models. By combining the last four categories, the new difficulty is essentially the proportion of endorsers (originally individuals in four ascending categories). So, if the graded response model is cumulative and derives threshold probabilities from the difference between the probabilities of two adjacent variables, shouldn't a dichotomized scale with the same initial category but fully combined ascending categories be equivalent to its polytomous version?

Even here, the only appliable DIF analysis relates to:

1- Conﬁgural Invariance [ equivalence of model form]

2- Weak Invariance [weak factorial - equivalence of factor loadings]

3- Strong Invariance [strong factorial - equivalence of item intercepts or thresholds]

If my understanding is appropriate. It's not possible to test DIF in 3PL models. What could we do in situations like that?

Second, to carry out a DIF analysis, we (still) can go with the multipleGroup function and then compare each model with an anova. such as anova(mod_configural,mod_metric).

However, it's also possible to check all items by using DIF and DTF and DRF functions. Even after reading your article (may not make a big DIF) and this thread here (https://groups.google.com/g/mirt-package/c/n_qj1GEQdz0/m/yX-t7-hnCgAJ), it's hard to interpret the output. For DIF, it's not so difficult, as significant P-values reveal a different functioning. Can you provide another reference to understand the difference between these analysis?

library(dplyr)

library(mirt)

ds_phil <- read.csv("~/ds_phil.csv")

# classic

# Groups

group <- ds_phil %>%

  select(sex) %>%

  arrange(sex) %>%

  mutate(sex = as.factor(sex)) %>%

set.seed(1)

  arrange(sex) %>%

  select(-sex) %>%

#check model estimates

M2(mod_configural)

I think you have it the other way around. SEM can be used to test DIF in 2PL/graded models if we use the three-step approach based on the polychoric correlation matrix methods (e.g., lavaan's categorical = ... input). The above three steps is all that you would need to evaluate the DIF strength. However, IRT can test DIF in 2PL/graded models + any other IRT model in existence, because DIF is just about evaluating whether the probability functions are equal across all possibility latent trait levels.

P(y|ψF,θ) =  P(y|ψR,θ)

for all values off θ. Often that can be tested directly based on the difference in the parameter sets, which if the parameters are unlikely to be equal (and items have the same functional form) then the probability functions  necessarily differ somewhere, and therefore DIF exists. Hence, you can certainly test for DIF using 3PL models, and in the likelihood testing framework this amounts to evaluating whether the parameters for a given item are likely/unlikely to be equal across groups. There may not be coined names for such tests (e.g., Step 4 - Pseudo-guessing Invariance), but the concept is the same.

messages.subject_clean: Multiple group analysis with longitudinal data
messages.body_plain:
If you have individuals who only exist in one time point then you should only need to place NA placeholders in the time points they didn't answer, and your dataset should consist of one participant's response vector per row (NAs included). If you stack the participants and record time as a type of grouping effect it's ignoring the within-subject correlation, and would be akin to treating a paired-samples t-test setup as a one-way t-test (if that helps conceptualize the issues using a more common statistical test). The MML estimator in mirt is not biased by missing data (it's actually quite efficient) so long as the data are truly missing at random. HTH.

Phil

My guess would have been to just use the expected item probabilities and subtract it from one (i.e., 1-P). And I found out that this can by achieved by flipping both the a and d-parameter.

I'm not aware of discussing what to do about the intercept parameters when flipping. Most often questions arise about the signs of the standardized loadings matrix and how those coefficients can be flipped meaningfully, which is agnostic to whatever the intercept parameters would be upon -1 multiplication.

>
> So now I am confused as to what to do, i.e. what is the correct way of going about this, multiplying the

>

The code below essentially calculates expected item probabilities (it is a multidimensional 2PL model with 2 traits), I calculate an expected prob for a medium score (theta = 0) and high (theta=4) score.
>
>
>

> # these are the parameters I got after my calibration (before which I reverse coded items)
> a=1.842
> d=0.342
>
> theta_mid<-c(0,0)
> theta_hi<-c(4,0)
>
> 1/ (1+exp(-1*(c(a,0)%*%theta_mid+ d))) # 0.5846763
> 1/ (1+exp(-1*(c(a,0)%*%theta_hi+ d))) #  0.9995519
>
> # only flipping a
> 1/ (1+exp(-1*(c(-a,0)%*%theta_mid+ d))) #0.5846763  NOTE THAT THIS IS THE SAME EXPECTED PROB AS ABOVE
> 1/ (1+exp(-1*(c(-a,0)%*%theta_hi+ d))) #0.0008876899 this is different
>
> # only flipping d

> 1/ (1+exp(-1*(c(a,0)%*%theta_mid+ -d))) #0.4153237 (NOTE THAT THIS IS 1 MINUS the above .58 prob)

> 1/ (1+exp(-1*(c(a,0)%*%theta_hi+ -d))) #0.9991123 (NOTE THAT THIS IS 1 MINUS the above .000887 prob)
>
> # flipping both a and d

> 1/ (1+exp(-1*(c(-a,0)%*%theta_hi+ -d))) # 0.0004481206 (SAME AS 1-0.9995519 FROM ABOVE)

>
>

Select the method that is invariant to the data transformation you're performing and would give the complement of the original expected probability functions (in this case, the -1 multiplication of all parameters). Which, of course, can be verified with a little code:

`````
library(mirt)
theta <- -6:6

dat1 <- dat2 <- expand.table(LSAT7)
dat2[,1] <- abs(dat1[,1] - 1)

mod1 <- mirt(dat1, 1)
coef(mod1, simplify=TRUE)
eprob1 <- probtrace(extract.item(mod1, 1), theta)

mod2 <- mirt(dat2, 1)
coef(mod2, simplify=TRUE) #both signs flipped
eprob2 <- probtrace(extract.item(mod2, 1), theta)

data.frame(theta, original=eprob1, reverse=eprob2)
````

> >
> > Therefore, I took some days looking for this subject here in the google forum, and then I would like to clarify 2 points with you. I'll write some questions and if you could just confirm if my understanding is correct, it will be great.
> >
> >
> > First, in IRT framework, it's possible to use the same framework used in SEM if we are dealing with 2PL (and Graded) models-only. (I've got from here: https://groups.google.com/g/mirt-package/c/MDbY0OkUMSY/m/w_PmzHEWBgAJ)
> >
> >
> > Even here, the only appliable DIF analysis relates to:
> >
> > 1- Conﬁgural Invariance [ equivalence of model form]
> >
> > 2- Weak Invariance [weak factorial - equivalence of factor loadings]
> >
> > 3- Strong Invariance [strong factorial - equivalence of item intercepts or thresholds]
> >
> >
> > If my understanding is appropriate. It's not possible to test DIF in 3PL models. What could we do in situations like that?
>
> I think you have it the other way around. SEM can be used to test DIF in 2PL/graded models if we use the three-step approach based on the polychoric correlation matrix methods (e.g., lavaan's categorical = ... input). The above three steps is all that you would need to evaluate the DIF strength. However, IRT can test DIF in 2PL/graded models + any other IRT model in existence, because DIF is just about evaluating whether the probability functions are equal across all possibility latent trait levels.
>
> P(y|ψF,θ) =  P(y|ψR,θ)
>
> for all values off θ. Often that can be tested directly based on the difference in the parameter sets, which if the parameters are unlikely to be equal (and items have the same functional form) then the probability functions  necessarily differ somewhere, and therefore DIF exists. Hence, you can certainly test for DIF using 3PL models, and in the likelihood testing framework this amounts to evaluating whether the parameters for a given item are likely/unlikely to be equal across groups. There may not be coined names for such tests (e.g., Step 4 - Pseudo-guessing Invariance), but the concept is the same.
>
> >
> > Second, to carry out a DIF analysis, we (still) can go with the multipleGroup function and then compare each model with an anova. such as anova(mod_configural,mod_metric).
> >
> > However, it's also possible to check all items by using DIF and DTF and DRF functions. For DIF, it's not so difficult, as significant P-values reveal a different functioning. Can you provide another reference to understand the difference between these analysis?
> All of these functions suggest differing response functional forms. If you haven't read my article with respecto the DRF statistics I'd recommend that first, as it may answer some of your questions and reveal the different between the DTF and DRF statistics.
>
>
> >
> >
> > Third and last, if I did all analysis correctly, my results seem strange. I have a dataset (attached), formed of 1326 participants. When I run a multigroup analysis, the metric invariance was *not* preserved

> >
> >     SE = TRUE)
> >
> > Model 2: multipleGroup(data = ., model = 1, group = group)
> >
> >
> >        AIC AICc SABIC HQ BIC logLik X2 df p
> >
> > 1 29207.87 29219.37 29376.99 29371.28 29643.82 -14519.93 NaN NaN NaN
> >
> > 2 29164.25 29185.12 29389.75 29382.13 29745.52 -14470.12 99.617 28 0
> >
> >
> > However, the scalar (strong) was.

> >
> >     "intercepts", "free_var", "free_means"),
> >
> >     SE = TRUE)

>

To evaluate DIF using this approach you would just need to loop over each item and free the parameters for each respective item, and likely apply some family-wise error adjustment for the exploratory data snooping. This is actually what's automated in the DIF() function when using the 'drop' scheme. For this reason I'll avoid running your code below since I believe it's unnecessary.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dr. Chalmers,

I created my final mirt model- a random group by item interaction with a condition slope effect:

items = colnames(data[,5:26])
data$Condition = factor(data$Condition)
data$Condition = revalue(data$Condition, "1" = Baseline, "2" = PostCondition)
model = mixedmirt(data[5:26], 1, random = ~Condition|items:Sex, itemtype = "Rasch", covdata = data[,2:3])

I believe with this model, I am able to execute my initial idea - modeling DIF caused by the interaction of sex in the pre and post condition thus obtaining accurate theta's. I looked at the random and fixed design matrices of my model and I see that every individual has the same fixed model intercept with random deviations/DIF that depends on group membership. Additionally, randef(model) produces two columns for my item by group interaction with a Condition slope and I noticed that the first column is essentially
the deviations of Baseline males and females from the fixed intercept and the second column are the delta's. Finally, from randef, I extracted the theta's to use in other statistical analysis.

Ultimately, I wanted to ask if for this model, mirt is able to separate latent group differences from DIF. I conducted miniature tests, where I select an individual's thetas extracted from randef, and calculate the probability of an individual to see if it is approximately equal to total score,Probability = 1/(1 + exp (-1(Latent Ability + Fixed Intercept + Baseline Deviation + PostCondition DeviationX)). From these results, everything looks good, it seems as if I properly informed mirt that an individual's theta is conditional on the random effect - "Condition|items:Sex" and it has recognized that their are four groups (Baseline Males, Baseline Females, PostCondition Males, and Post Condition Females). I'm interested in using mixedmirt to estimate a MIMIC-type model, where a continuous predictor (a personality trait) predicts both the item intercepts as well as the item discrimination/slope parameters.

A model like:  P(x = 1 | θ, ψ) = 1 / (1 + exp(-1 * [θ * (a + ψζ) +  ψβ))

For example, I might have a set of cognitive test items, and I want to model the effects of test anxiety scores on both item difficulties and discrimination parameters.

I could potentially extend this to include random effects as well ala https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11336-013-9360-2.pdf

Can item discrimination models currently be estimated in mirt? From the ?mixedmirt documentation, it seems like only intercept models can be specified.

Using the `lr.fixed` and `lr.random` arguments, I could specify a model for θ, but that is a slightly different specification than specifying a model for a directly (e.g., if I wanted to estimate both non-uniform DIF and latent trait group differences).

Thanks!
